prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My mother the queen is dead. My father the king is old. He fumbles his cirque of gold And dreams of a year long fled. The young men stare at my face, But cannot meet my glance— Cavan tall as a lance, Orra swift in the race. Death was ever my price, Since my maidenhood began: At the thought of a Gaelic man My heart is sister of ice. ’Tis another for whom I wait, Though I have not kissed his sword: He or none is my lord, Though our night be soon or late. The star grows great in my breast: It is crying clearly now To the star on the burnished prow Of his galley far in the West. The capes of the North are dim, And the windward beaches smoke Where the last long roller spoke The tidings it held of him. Sorrow I know he brings, Battle, despair and change,— Beauty cruel and strange, And the shed bright blood of kings. Breast, be white for his sake! Mouth, be red for the kiss! Soul, be strong for your bliss! Heart, be ready to break!

# The Waiting Queen

My mother the queen lies dead.
My father the king grows old,
And fumbles his crown of gold,
Dreaming of years long fled.

The young men gaze on my face,
Yet cannot hold my glance—
Cavan, tall as a lance,
Orra, swift in the race.

Death has been my due
Since first my maidenhood came:
At the thought of a Gaelic name
My heart turns cold and true.

’Tis another for whom I wait,
Though I have not touched his sword:
He, and none else, my lord,
Be our meeting soon or late.

The star swells bright in my breast,
Calling with voice unconfined
To the star on the prow behind—
His galley far in the West.

The northern capes lie dim,
The windward beaches smoke
Where the last long roller spoke
The tidings it bore of him.

Sorrow, I know, he will bring—
Battle, despair, and change,
Beauty cruel and strange,
And the bright blood shed of a king.

Breast, grow pale for his sake!
Lips, blush red for the kiss!
Soul, stand firm for such bliss!
Heart, be ready to break!
outputs.L2:
**My Own Rendering:**

My mother, the sovereign lady, has passed. My father, the aged monarch, sits weary—his crown of gold slips from trembling hands as memory carries him to seasons long vanished.

Young suitors gaze upon my features, yet none can hold my eyes: Cavan, towering as a spear-shaft, Orra, fleet-footed as wind itself.

Since girlhood's dawn, mortality has always been my rightful cost. When any native-born man draws near in thought, my heart turns to ice, cold as a distant kin.

No, I await a different one entirely—though I've never touched his blade in greeting. He shall be my only master, whether our meeting comes swiftly or slow.

Within my chest a star swells, calling out—reaching toward its twin upon the gleaming prow of his ship, still far off in western waters.

The northern headlands blur into mist, and smoke drifts along the windswept shore where the final great wave whispered word of his coming.

I know well the gifts he carries: grief, warfare, upheaval entire—a beauty both merciless and foreign, and the bright royal blood soon to be spilled.

Let my breast turn pale in his honor! Let my lips flush crimson for his kiss! Let my spirit rise strong to meet its joy! Let my heart stand ready for its breaking!
outputs.L3:
# The Waiting Princess

The queen my mother sleeps beneath the cold earth now, her voice silenced, her laughter but a memory that haunts these ancient halls. My father, once a king of fire and command, has become a shadow of his former majesty—an old man wrapped in furs by the hearth, his eyes clouded with the mists of yesterday, forever wandering through corridors of memory that only he can see. The court moves around him now, as if he were already a ghost among the living.

And so it falls to me to carry what remains of our house's fate.

They come to me, these young men of our own soil—Cavan with his easy smile, Orra with his practiced words of devotion. They kneel, they praise, they offer their hearts as though love were a simple thing, a gift easily given and easily received. Yet I feel nothing when I look upon them. No flutter, no warmth, no answering call within my breast. For every Gaelic suitor who has ever sought my hand, I have learned this bitter truth: death alone has been my price, the toll exacted from those who dare to love a princess such as I. Their devotion withers before my indifference, and still my heart remains untouched, waiting for something—someone—I cannot yet name.

For I do not wait for them. I wait for a stranger whose face I have never seen, whose voice I have never heard, whose name remains a mystery even to my dreams. Somewhere in the vast darkness of the western sea, upon a galley I cannot see but somehow know exists, a star burns for me alone. It calls across the impossible distance, a beacon meant only for my eyes, summoning me toward a destiny I cannot refuse even if I wished to.

Already the signs gather like storm clouds on the horizon. From the northern coasts, whispers travel on the wind—strange omens, unfamiliar portents that speak of his approach. I feel him drawing nearer with each passing day, though I could not say how I know this truth. And with his coming, I sense not joy alone but something far more complex: sorrow woven through with splendor, battle's brutal music mixed with beauty so strange and cruel it defies description. Royal blood will spill before this tale finds its ending—I know this as surely as I know my own name. Yet still I wait, still I watch the western waters, unable to turn away from what fate has written for me.

So let it come, this union both blessed and cursed. I prepare myself now in every part of my being—my body readied for whatever transformation awaits, my mouth prepared for words of welcome or perhaps a final farewell to the girl I once was, my soul steeling itself against the storm to come, my heart opening despite every warning whispered by reason and caution alike. I will meet this fate with open arms, embracing both the ecstasy that calls to me from across the dark waters and the heartbreak I know must follow in its wake. For this is my destiny, foretold in stars and shadows both—and I will not turn away from what has been written for me since before my birth.

# The Princess by the Sea

The tower window frames her days,
a portrait carved in patient stone,
where she watches horizons blaze
with sunsets she must face alone.

Her father's kingdom, once so grand,
now shows its age in crumbling walls—
the banners droop, the loyal band
of courtiers thin as autumn falls.

Princes come from neighboring lands,
with gifts of gold and honeyed words,
they kneel and offer heart and hands,
but she has heard what she has heard:

A prophecy the stars once told,
of one who'd cross the churning deep,
a lord not born of native mold,
whose coming she's sworn now to keep.

She turns away the noble sons
who press their suits with practiced grace—
their kingdoms small, their battles won
seem hollow when she dreams of space,

of endless water, endless sky,
a ship emerging from the mist,
a stranger's love she can't deny
though logic says this can't exist.

The elders whisper of her folly,
waiting for a ghost, a myth,
while youth slips by in melancholy—
but she remains steadfast, and with

each passing star that marks the night,
she feels the pull of destiny,
knows somehow that her fatal plight
is written in the rolling sea.

For love this vast, this strange, this true,
must carry weight of tragedy—
the greater joy that waits construe
the deeper grief that's meant to be.

She does not fear the coming pain,
the way transcendent love destroys
the ordinary, mundane reign
of safer, smaller earthly joys.

So still she waits, though kingdoms fade,
though suitors turn to bitter foes,
though father's crown begins to shade
to rust beneath the wind that blows.

Because she knows—she's always known—
that when his ship breaks through the fog,
she'll finally cease to feel alone,
though doom sits waiting like a dog

beside the shore, patient and true,
as certain as the tide's return—
she'll pay love's debt, whatever's due,
and in his arms, she'll gladly burn.
outputs.L5:
# The Waiting Room

Sarah had been sitting in the plastic chair for forty minutes. **And** the clock on the wall seemed to move slower with each passing second. **The** magazines on the table beside her were outdated, their covers featuring celebrities from years past. **But** she couldn't bring herself to pick one up anyway.

Her phone buzzed with a message from her sister. **And** she smiled despite the anxiety twisting in her stomach. **The** words on the screen offered comfort—simple reassurances that everything would be fine. **But** deep down, she knew that no one could truly promise that.

**The** nurse finally called her name, breaking the silence that had settled over the room. **And** Sarah felt her heart rate quicken as she stood up. **But** she reminded herself to breathe, to stay calm, to trust the process that had brought her this far.

Walking down the corridor, she thought about all the moments that had led to this point. **The** late nights researching, the conversations with doctors, the difficult decisions. **And** through it all, she had remained determined. **But** determination alone couldn't guarantee the outcome she hoped for.

**The** door to the examination room opened, **and** light poured through the window onto the sterile floor. **But** in that moment, Sarah felt something shift inside her—not certainty, but a quiet acceptance. Whatever news awaited her, she would face it with the same strength that had carried her this far.

**The** waiting was almost over. **And** whatever came next, she was ready.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a Celtic princess awaiting a mysterious foreign warrior destined to bring both love and doom.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Waiting

I stand upon the weathered stones tonight,
where mist curls up from valleys steeped in gray,
and watch the western sky surrender light
to darkness creeping in from far away.

The druids read the omens in the flame,
and spoke of one who comes from foreign shore—
a warrior bearing neither shield nor name
I know, yet know I've waited for before.

My father's torque of gold weighs on my breast,
a princess bound by duty, blood, and land,
yet something wild stirs within my chest
that no betrothal ever quite has spanned.

The ravens gather in the ancient oak,
their black wings folded like a held-back word.
The old wife by the fire has softly spoke
of love that comes as sword and as reward.

I do not know his face, his tongue, his creed,
only that when he comes, the world will bend—
that what he brings will answer some deep need,
and carry with it whispers of an end.

Still I will climb these stones each fading day,
and let the sea wind tangle in my hair,
for fate has never asked which path or way
we'd choose, if choosing were within our care.

Come, stranger, with your doom wrapped up in grace—
I've dreamed you longer than I've drawn a breath.
Let me look once upon your foreign face
before you teach me how to love, and death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal, rhymed lyric poem with a mythic Irish/Gaelic setting, featuring a dying king, a dead queen, and a prophetic daughter.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Keening at Dún na Ríogh**

Beneath the yew where ravens cry,
And cold loch-water laps the shore,
Queen Aoife's bones in stillness lie,
Who ruled these hills a year before.

They wound her in a cloak of moss,
They sang no dirge, for none dared sing,
And since that day of bitter loss
The grief has gnawed her lord and king.

Now Conall, king of that far land,
Lies fevered on his oaken bed,
The torc grown loose upon his hand,
The crown too heavy for his head.

His daughter Síne keeps the watch,
Whose eyes are grey as winter storm—
For she was born beneath a notch
Of moon that shaped her secret form.

"I see," she said, "a ship of bone
Come sailing up the river Bann,
I see a stranger take the throne,
And weep for it, poor drownèd man.

"The hall shall fall, the fire go dark,
The harp-string snap at pale moonrise,
Yet from this ash shall leap a spark
To light the road to Otherwise.

"For every king the earth has hid
Beneath her quiet, patient stone
Walks after in the land of Sidh,
And waits there for his own, his own."

He died as dies an ember's spark
Between the telling and the dawn,
And Síne lit no torch nor mark,
But let him pass as kings have gone.

Unmourned by trumpet, urged by none,
Save wind that combs the barley down,
And she who watched the sinking sun
Take with it both her sire and crown.

Now Síne walks the strand alone,
Her mother's cairn, her father's grave,
Two mounds beneath the wide unknown,
And she the only word they gave—

The last to know what green tide brings,
The first to name the coming year,
The daughter of two buried kings,
Who speaks, and no one living hears.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem imitating early 20th-century fantasy poets like Lord Dunsany or James Stephens, with archaic diction and a doomed heroine?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Weaving of Ilmarel**

Beyond the hills of Sarn-i-Dûr,
where twilight never turns to day,
there dwelt a maid, Ilmarel the pure,
who wove her doom in threads of grey.

Her father was a king of dust,
his throne a barrow, his crown a stone;
her mother, in the old gods' trust,
had given her breath, then turned to bone.

She sat beside the Loom of Years
and spun what Fate had bid her spin—
a tapestry of nights and fears,
wherein no thread of gold was in.

"O maiden, cease," the grey wind cried,
"for what thou weav'st, thy death shall be."
She only smiled, and shook her head:
"I weave what I was born to see."

There came a knight from Almoreth,
with sword of frost and eyes of flame;
he begged her leave the Loom of Death
and ride with him from whence he came.

"Nay," said she, "for threads once begun
must to their ending be pursued;
I am not thine, nor anyone's,
but Fate's own handmaid, dark-imbued."

He rode away ere morning broke,
and she wove on till candle's end,
till the last thread beneath her broke,
and shadow came to be her friend.

They found her there when stars were thin,
her tapestry complete and cold—
a pattern of where death begins,
worked all in silver, black, and gold.

Now in that hall no torches burn,
no minstrel sings her doomed renown,
save wind that through the arches turns
and whispers low: *the thread wore down.*

---

I tried to capture that particular Dunsany/Stephens mood—fate as a kind of craft or duty, a heroine who accepts doom with quiet dignity rather than resisting it, and a world just slightly askew from our own (invented geography, gods "long overthrown," that pervasive twilight). Happy to adjust the meter, lengthen it into more of a ballad narrative, or lean harder into whimsy (more Stephens) versus cosmic melancholy (more Dunsany) if you'd like a different balance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a ballad-style poem about a princess who refuses local suitors because she senses her true, fateful love arriving by ship from the West.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Princess of the Western Wind

By the cliffs where salt winds gather,
Sat a princess, fair and lone,
While her father's hall grew weary
Of the suitors she'd not own.

Lords had come with gold and promise,
Knights with banners bright unfurled,
Princes from the eastern kingdoms,
Merchants from the southern world.

"Daughter, why do you refuse them?"
Asked the king with troubled brow.
"Every noble house has offered—
Will you not choose one for spouse?"

She would only gaze westward,
Where the sun sank into foam,
"There's a love that comes to find me,
One whose face I've never known.

I have dreamed him in the harbor,
Standing tall against the mast,
With the sea-spray in his shadow,
Sailing toward me, free at last.

I can feel him crossing waters,
Feel the distance growing thin,
Some fates are not born of choosing—
Mine will simply enter in."

So she turned away the lordlings,
Turned away the crowns of gold,
While her father shook his head at
Dreams he thought too wild, too bold.

Seasons turned to years in waiting,
Still she walked the cliffside stone,
Still she watched the empty water,
Still she stood her watch alone.

Then one dawn when mist hung heavy,
Silver on the sleeping sea,
Came a ship with sails like moonlight,
Drifting soft as prophecy.

And a stranger stood upon it,
Weathered by a thousand tides,
With a gaze that met her waiting
Like the moon meets rising tide.

No word passed between the watchers,
Yet she knew him, knew him true—
Not a name that she had spoken,
But a soul she'd always knew.

Let them say she was but foolish,
Let them call her dreams unwise—
Some hearts read their fate in far winds,
Some see futures in the skies.

For the princess of the headland
Knew what waited past the foam:
Love arrives when it arrives to,
Not by will, but coming home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short narrative poem in quatrains, ABBA or ABAB rhyme, with themes of prophecy, tragic love, and Celtic royal lineage.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Daughter of Kells

The druid spoke beneath the yew,
"A queen shall rise when ravens fall,
Her heart shall break for one she'll rue,
And blood shall mark her father's hall."

Young Deirdre heard the prophecy,
And laughed, for she was but sixteen,
She knew not what her fate would be,
Nor how her love would break a queen.

She met a warrior, Conall named,
Of lowborn stock, not royal line,
Her father's court called it a shame,
Forbade their hearts from intertwine.

"I am the blood of ancient kings,"
She told her love beneath the moon,
"Yet crowns are cold and empty things
Compared to what our hearts have hewn."

They fled by night past standing stones,
Past cairns where elder spirits sleep,
But armies came to claim the throne,
And blood was spilled both wide and deep.

Her father's men found Conall first,
Cut down before her weeping eyes,
The prophecy fulfilled its curse—
The raven king had claimed his prize.

She took the blade meant for her love,
And turned it toward her breaking heart,
"No crown," she cried to stars above,
"Is worth this life ripped clean apart."

So Deirdre died as ravens rose,
Her royal blood soaked Kells' own ground,
The druids sang of love and woes,
Of prophecy in sorrow drowned.

Now bards still sing of Deirdre's fate,
Of Celtic blood and broken vow,
How love can shatter crown and state—
Her ghost still walks the hillside now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
